newsitem.title: GERMANY: Allianz, Dresdner funds link a smart move-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Allianz, Dresdner funds link a smart move-analysts.

text.p: Plans for Germany's Allianz AG and Dresdner Bank AG to rev up their long-standing alliance should prove a smart strategic choice which could see them join forces to buy an asset manager, analysts said on Wednesday.

The plans emerged on Tuesday as Dresdner stressed the strategic importance of its ties with Allianz, which owns over 22 percent of the bank, and said the companies were mulling more links in areas such as asset management -- a growing segment viewed worldwide as a top income generator.

Analysts say Dresdner, already viewed as a global player in asset management with assets under management of 330 billion marks ($179.6 billion), would bring useful expertise to such a venture. Allianz, Europe's second largest insurance group, would bring clout and buying power.

"After all the changes in the German banking scene, Allianz will be focusing more and more on its relationship with Dresdner," said Trevor May, insurance analyst at Salomon Brothers. "Right now it is basically building up expertise for the future."
For Dresdner, tighter links with Allianz would reinforce its position in an industry hell-bent on consolidation.
Together, the two German companies would form a counterweight to the rival banking and insurance groups presided over by Deutsche Bank AG.
"More co-operations between banks and insurance firms will develop in Germany and they are necessary in this increasingly international market," said Commerzbank analyst Dieter Hein.

Dresdner currently faces being ousted from the number two position in German commercial banking after last week's decision by Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechsel-Bank AG to join forces to form a giant Munich-based bank.

While tighter ties with Allianz may not herald another German mega-merger -- and analysts think a complete fusion is unlikely at present -- it will cement Dresdner's relationship with its insurance partner, with whom it has long had a sales agreement.
"What we have here is a larger financial group and it cannot be ruled out that the two together might find acquisitions - perhaps in France, that would suit both of them," said Commerzbank's Hein.
Analysts also see Dresdner as offering Allianz a level of global investment management expertise that the insurance giant currently lacks, but needs to acquire.

Increased investor sophistication has left banks and insurers increasingly competing head to head, as more and more investors opt for mutual funds and other pooled investments as alternatives to traditional life insurance cover.
Allianz itself has some 344 billion marks in investments under management but analysts view its relatively limited business on behalf of outside clients as being ripe for expansion.
"Allianz has made clear that it wants to make some kind of quantum leap in asset management," said Simon Foessmeier, analyst at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt.
"This is a real area where co-operation with a bank would make sense."
Allianz boasts that its products are sold over 11,000 bank counters worldwide and has been at the forefront of a push to forge closer links between banking and insurance in general.

About one in five new Allianz life insurance policies are sold over bank counters in Germany and the insurer has made clear that it is also interested in broadening the scope of its asset management activities.

"We really have to check every day whether our definition of core business is still valid," Allianz chief executive Henning Schulte-Noelle told Germany's Finanz und Wirtschft magazine earlier this year.
"We see that in some areas, the boundaries between banking and insurance are fading."
The implications of such a statement by one of Europe's most influential insurance executives are unclear.
Some analysts have predicted a gradual fusion of banking and insurance business in Germany, moving toward giant financial conglomerages such as ING in the Netherlands.
But not all observers are convinced.
"Apart from ING there is really no insurer with a major role in banking," said Julius Baer's Foessmeier.
